figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Illustration of memory importance in AI agents. Left: Without persistent memory, the system forgets critical user information (vegetarian, dairy-free preferences) between sessions, resulting in inappropriate recommendations. Right: With effective memory, the system maintains these dietary preferences across interactions, enabling contextually appropriate suggestions that align with previously established constraints.
figures.headline: Without persistent memory the system suggests chicken to a vegetarian user, while with memory it suggests dairy-free vegetarian options.
citing_sentences: Consider a simple example illustrated in Figure 1, where a user mentions being vegetarian and avoiding dairy products in an initial conversation.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Architectural overview of the Mem0 system showing extraction and update phase. The extraction phase processes messages and historical context to create new memories. The update phase evaluates these extracted memories against similar existing ones, applying appropriate operations through a Tool Call mechanism. The database serves as the central repository, providing context for processing and storing updated memories.
figures.headline: The Mem0 pipeline runs an extraction phase that builds candidate memories, then an update phase that adds, updates, deletes or skips each one.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Figure 2, the complete pipeline architecture consists of two phases: extraction and update.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Graph-based memory architecture of $\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}$ illustrating entity extraction and update phase. The extraction phase uses LLMs to convert conversation messages into entities and relation triplets. The update phase employs conflict detection and resolution mechanisms when integrating new information into the existing knowledge graph.
figures.headline: The graph pipeline turns messages into entity and relation triplets, then applies conflict detection and resolution when merging them into the graph.
citing_sentences: The $\texttt{Mem0}^{\tiny g}$ pipeline, illustrated in Figure 3, implements a graph-based memory approach that effectively captures, stores, and retrieves contextual information from natural language interactions (Zhang et al., 2022).

Subfigure (a) highlights the search/retrieval latency prior to answer generation, while Subfigure (b) shows the total latency (including LLM inference). Both plots overlay each method’s J score for a holistic view of their accuracy and efficiency.

Our proposed Mem0 approach achieves the lowest search latency among all methods (p50: 0.148s, p95: 0.200s) as illustrated in Figure 4(a).

abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable prowess in generating contextually coherent responses, yet their fixed context windows pose fundamental challenges for maintaining consistency over prolonged multi-session dialogues. We introduce Mem0, a scalable memory-centric architecture that addresses this issue by dynamically extracting, consolidating, and retrieving salient information from ongoing conversations. Building on this foundation, we further propose an enhanced variant that leverages graph-based memory representations to capture complex relational structures among conversational elements. Through comprehensive evaluations on the LOCOMO benchmark, we systematically compare our approaches against six baseline categories: (i) established memory-augmented systems, (ii) retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with varying chunk sizes and $k$-values, (iii) a full-context approach that processes the entire conversation history, (iv) an open-source memory solution, (v) a proprietary model system, and (vi) a dedicated memory management platform. Empirical results demonstrate that our methods consistently outperform all existing memory systems across four question categories: single-hop, temporal, multi-hop, and open-domain. Notably, Mem0 achieves 26% relative improvements in the LLM-as-a-Judge metric over OpenAI, while Mem0 with graph memory achieves around 2% higher overall score than the base Mem0 configuration. Beyond accuracy gains, we also markedly reduce computational overhead compared to the full-context approach. In particular, Mem0 attains a 91% lower p95 latency and saves more than 90% token cost, thereby offering a compelling balance between advanced reasoning capabilities and practical deployment constraints. Our findings highlight the critical role of structured, persistent memory mechanisms for long-term conversational coherence, paving the way for more reliable and efficient LLM-driven AI agents.

Code can be found at: https://mem0.ai/research

sections.body: The introduction argues that fixed context windows make LLM agents forget user facts across sessions, using a vegetarian example. It says longer windows only delay the problem, because conversation history exceeds context limits and topics shift, and attention degrades over distant tokens. The authors introduce Mem0, which dynamically captures, organizes and retrieves salient information from ongoing conversations, and a graph-based variant that models relationships between conversational elements. They report better results than existing memory systems on the LOCOMO benchmark, and a 91% lower response time than full-context approaches.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Fixed context windows make AI agents forget user facts across sessions, so the paper proposes persistent memory systems, Mem0 and a graph-based variant.

sections.body: Mem0 processes each new message pair in two phases. The extraction phase builds a prompt from a conversation summary, recent messages and the new pair, and an LLM extracts candidate facts. The update phase retrieves the top s similar memories for each fact and lets the LLM choose add, update, delete or skip through a tool-call interface. The graph variant stores memories as directed labeled graphs with entities as nodes and relationships as edges, extracted by LLMs. An LLM-based resolver marks conflicting relationships as invalid rather than deleting them. Retrieval combines entity-centric subgraph search with triplet similarity matching.
sections.heading: Proposed Methods
sections.headline: Mem0 extracts candidate facts from message pairs and updates memory through add, update, delete or skip decisions; the graph variant stores entities and relations.

sections.body: The LOCOMO dataset has 10 extended conversations of about 26000 tokens on average, with about 200 questions each across single-hop, multi-hop, temporal and open-domain types. The adversarial category is excluded because ground truth answers were unavailable. Answers are scored with F1, BLEU-1 and LLM-as-a-Judge, and the judge scores are reported as the mean over 10 runs with one standard deviation. The six baseline categories are established LOCOMO benchmarks, open-source memory, RAG with chunk sizes from 128 to 8192 tokens and k of 1 or 2, full-context processing, a proprietary memory feature, and a memory platform. The text notes that lexical metrics can miss factual errors.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: The paper tests on the LOCOMO benchmark, scoring answers with lexical overlap metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge against six baseline categories.

sections.body: Table 1 compares F1, B1 and J across question types. Mem0 reports J 67.13 on single-hop and J 51.15 on multi-hop questions, the highest in those types. The graph variant reports J 58.13 on temporal questions, above Mem0 at 55.51. On open-domain questions, Zep reports J 76.60, above the graph variant at 75.71 and Mem0 at 72.93. Table 2 gives Mem0 a search latency p50 of 0.148 seconds and a total p95 of 1.440 seconds, against 17.117 seconds for full-context. The graph variant reports an overall J of 68.44%. The text notes that graph memory gave no gain on multi-hop questions.
sections.heading: Evaluation Results, Analysis and Discussion.
sections.headline: Mem0 leads single-hop and multi-hop questions, the graph variant leads temporal questions, and Zep leads open-domain questions among compared systems.

sections.body: The conclusion states that Mem0 performs best on single-hop and multi-hop reasoning, while the graph variant gives gains on temporal and open-domain tasks. It reports relative improvements of 5%, 11% and 7% in single-hop, temporal and multi-hop questions over the best method in each type. It also reports a p95 latency reduction of over 91% against full-context baselines. Stated future work includes reducing latency overhead in the graph variant, hierarchical memory architectures, better consolidation mechanisms, and extending the frameworks to procedural reasoning and multimodal interactions.
sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
sections.headline: The conclusion claims a balance of accuracy and latency, and names graph operation overhead and non-conversational domains as future work.

sections.body: Appendix A says the LLM-as-a-Judge prompt adapts elements of a prompt released by Packer et al. (2023). Appendix B is titled Algorithm and has no text in the input, although the update phase is said to be illustrated there. Appendix C describes the selected baselines. LoCoMo uses session summaries, observations and a temporal event graph. ReadAgent uses episode pagination, memory gisting and interactive lookup. MemoryBank uses storage, retrieval and updating with a forgetting mechanism. MemGPT uses main and external context. A-Mem builds linked notes that evolve as new memories arrive.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the LLM-as-a-Judge prompt source, has an empty algorithm section, and describes the LoCoMo, ReadAgent, MemoryBank, MemGPT and A-Mem baselines.
